description_en: Ajayamerukoṭa is situated 4 km north-west of Amargaḍhī, the Dadeldhura district headquarters. Most of the monuments are built on the right bank of the Chaurī Gāḍ river, a tributary of the Mahakali (or Sharda) river, which forms the western border between India and Nepal. Other contemporary constructions in the vicinity include (DDL0110,DDL0111,DDL0112,DDL0113andDDL0120).The Ajayamerukoṭa area is known for its abundance of monuments, primarily constructed during the 14th and 15th centuries. According to D. P. Ojha, Ajayamerukoṭa served as a local capital for the Khasiya kings from Jumla, specifically the Khaśa Malla emperors of the 12th-14th century (Ojha 1989, p. 54). From the mid-14th century onwards, Ajayamerukoṭa gained greater importance as the capital of the Doti kingdom, particularly during the reign of King Niraya Pāla (approximately 1362-1383 AD). It was during this time that Doti emerged as an independent entity separate from the Khaśa Malla empire. The political and economic rise of the region is evidenced by the numerous monuments constructed during the latter half of the 14th century and throughout the 15th century.The monument in question is oriented towards the west. Its entrance is preceded by a pavilion (bhaiṭak, DDL0131), and across from the pavilion is another identicalśikharatemple (DDL0130). All three structures are erected on a shared stone platform.The monument has undergone reconstruction by Nepal's Department of Archaeology, as indicated by visible inventory numbers present throughout the structure. Therefore, it is possible that some elements may have been displaced, lost, or stolen. Blocks have been carved to replace missing ones.A intricately carvedjalaharīwith a makara head is placed at the base of the northern wall. This feature, used for pouring liquids such as milk and water overśivaliṅgas, suggests that the temple likely housed aśivaliṅgain its now-empty sanctum. The affiliation of the temple with the Śaiva tradition is further indicated by the presence of a Gaṇeśa carving in the middle part of the sanctum's door lintel.This architectural style, featuring a central pavilion (maṇḍapa,baiṭhak) flanked by twośikharas, is rarely found in far western Nepal but is seen at the Bhurtī Temple Complex in Dailekh district (DLK0015). However, there are structural differences between the Bhurtī and Ajayamerukoṭa monuments. In Bhurtī, the pavilion was intentionally integrated as a planned component of the temples, whereas in Ajayamerukoṭa, the pavilion appears as an independent structure. This suggests that the architects in Bhurtī were inspired by pre-existing models, such as the Ajayamerukoṭa monuments, which themselves were likely influenced by temples from Uttarakhand.Two inscriptions are engraved on the left side of the door. One of these inscriptions is dated to 1373 (ŚS 1295) and mentions King Niraya Pāla (Sharma 2012, p. 303).
references: REFERENCES Ojha, D. P. 1988. Doti Kṣetrako Itihās tathā Saṃnskrīti . Kathmandu: Sudur Paścimāncal Sāmājik Sevā tathā Anusandhān Samiti. Sharma, Dilli Raj. 2012. Heritage of Western Nepal. Art and Architecture . Kathmandu: Centre for Nepal and Asian Studies, pp. 302-304.
